groups.title: JavaScript language internals used throughout MEAN
groups.question: A teammate is surprised that a Promise callback runs before a setTimeout of zero, and that a click handler still remembers a variable from a function that already returned. Explain how JavaScript schedules work and keeps variables alive.

followUps.The event loop: call stack, microtasks,: Why does a resolved Promise's callback run before a setTimeout with zero delay?
followUps.Closures and lexical scoping in JavaScri: How does a handler keep access to a variable after its outer function returned?

evidence.text: JavaScript runs the current code on the call stack until it finishes.
Then it runs all queued microtasks, such as Promise callbacks.
Only after that does it take the next task, such as a timer callback.

misconceptions.text: Says setTimeout with zero delay runs immediately.

evidence.text: A closure is a function that keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created.
Which variables it can see is decided by where it is written, not where it is called.
Callbacks, services and RxJS operators all rely on closures.

notEnough: Only defining a closure as a function inside a function.

groups.title: Async patterns: Promises and async/await
groups.question: Your Node code loads a user, then their tasks and then their team, and one failure crashes the process. Explain how you would write this async code with Promises and async/await.

followUps.Promises: .then chaining, .catch, and Pr: What happens to a Promise chain when one step fails, and when would you use Promise.all?
followUps.async/await: syntactic sugar over Promis: How do you handle errors with async/await, and what happens if you do not?

evidence.text: then returns a new Promise, so steps can be chained.
A catch at the end handles a failure from any earlier step.
Promise.all runs independent work in parallel and rejects as soon as one input rejects.

notEnough: Only saying Promises handle async code.

misconceptions.text: Says Promise.all waits for every Promise even when one fails.

evidence.text: An async function always returns a Promise.
await pauses that function until the Promise settles.
Errors are caught with try and catch; an unhandled rejection can crash a Node process.

notEnough: Only saying async/await is cleaner syntax.

groups.title: ES6+ syntax used across the MEAN stack
groups.question: You are reading Angular and Node code full of destructuring, spread and imports, and a Node file fails with an error about require in an ES module. Explain these syntax features and the two module systems.

followUps.Destructuring, spread, and rest in funct: How are destructuring, spread and rest different?
followUps.ES modules: import/export and their diff: How do ES modules differ from CommonJS?

evidence.text: Destructuring pulls values out of objects and arrays into variables.
Spread copies or merges arrays and objects into a new one.
Rest collects the remaining arguments or properties into one variable.
ES modules use import and export, while CommonJS uses require and module.exports.
ES module imports are analyzed before the code runs, while require runs at runtime.
Mixing the two causes errors, so a project must know which system each file uses.

notEnough: Only saying ES modules are newer.

groups.title: DOM manipulation and responsive layout basics
groups.question: Before using Angular, you build a small task list with plain JavaScript that toggles a 'done' style on click and works on phones. Explain how you would handle the DOM and the layout.

followUps.DOM events, querySelector, and classList: How would you toggle a task's done state with plain JavaScript?
followUps.Flexbox and responsive layout with media: How would you lay out the list for phones first and wider screens later?

evidence.text: querySelector or querySelectorAll finds the elements.
addEventListener runs code on a click.
classList.toggle adds or removes a class that CSS uses to style the done state.

notEnough: Only saying you change the DOM.

evidence.text: Flexbox aligns items in a row or column, such as a task's text and its button.
Base styles target small screens.
min-width media queries add layout changes for larger screens.

notEnough: Only saying you use media queries.
